#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
A Transient Zone in the appearance of an old retro motel. Appearing in several cities at the same time. Rooms seem to switch and change at its own will.
The motel stood as a relic of a bygone era, its weary façade peeling paint and a faded neon sign announcing "The Roadside Lodge Motel." The dimly lit parking lot held a few scattered cars under a starless night sky. Each room had a solitary window, their curtains drawn to conceal the secrets within.
A flickering vacancy sign buzzed intermittently, casting eerie shadows that danced on the cracked pavement. Inside, the air held the faint scent of aged memories and stale cigarettes, a timeless aroma shared by all motels of its kind. It was a place where travellers stopped briefly, leaving little trace of their existence, and where the passage of time had rendered it no more than a stopover in the journey of countless others.

#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
The main location for the short story The Midnight Carnival (Short Story).
Nestled among the rugged peaks of the Midwest, Willowbrook was a mountain town that seemed to defy the norms of its surroundings. With a population that barely reached a few thousand, the town exuded an aura of peace and seclusion. Its residents were familiar faces, and in a place where everybody knew your name, a strong sense of community prevailed.
Willowbrook's architectural charm was a testament to its storied history. The town was graced with a delightful mix of old-world elegance and rustic simplicity. Historic building adorned with simple exteriors, built during the towns first settlement and heavily maintained were matched by the, then modern now older 80’s and early 90’s brick, concrete and working facades. The town’s main road was what you would expect from a small Midwest town. Lined with stores that had ran in the families of the occupiers since the towns beginnings as a lumber and mine settlement. ‘Old Jane's Hardware Store’, ‘Willowbrook General Store’ and ‘Wilkinson's & Sons Bakery’ some of the key stores of the town. No big chains, no big restaurants just a family run diner.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/citadel-of-.description:
#Character #CitadelOfDarknessCharacter
#Character #CitadelOfDarknessCharacter
Infobox
Chloe Harren is an orphan who slipped through the cracks long before anyone noticed she was falling. Her parents died in a house fire when she was six years old, an incident ruled accidental, quickly closed, and never spoken about in detail. Since then, Chloe has moved through the social care system like a ghost, passed from placement to placement, file to file, learning early that survival means being agreeable, forgettable, and quiet.
She is known in certain wealthy circles not directly, but by proxy, mentioned in conversations between social workers, sponsors, and patrons who frame their interest as charitable. To them, Chloe is a project, a cause, a fragile thing to be “saved.”
Chloe is slight and pale, with the kind of build that makes adults assume she’s younger than she is. Her hair is a muted, dusty blonde, usually worn loose or in a careless ponytail, as if styling it would be an unnecessary indulgence. It always looks a little unkempt, not from neglect, but from disinterest.
Her eyes are soft and observant, a washed-out hazel that rarely holds direct contact for long. There are faint shadows beneath them, the kind that never quite go away no matter how much she sleeps. Her expressions tend toward neutral, subdued, restrained, yet when she’s startled or afraid, it flashes across her face with startling clarity.
She dresses practically: hoodies, worn jackets, jeans that have been patched or replaced more than once. Nothing she owns draws attention. Even her posture seems designed to take up as little space as possible, shoulders slightly hunched, hands often tucked into sleeves or pockets like she’s bracing against the world.
Chloe is quiet, compliant, and painfully polite, not because she’s meek, but because she’s learned that compliance keeps her safe. She reads people quickly, instinctively adjusting her tone and behaviour to match what’s expected of her. Adults describe her as “well-behaved” and “easy,” unaware that this is a carefully constructed survival tactic.
Beneath the surface, Chloe is deeply observant. She notices small inconsistencies, shifts in mood, the way people look at her when they think she isn’t paying attention. She has an instinctive distrust of generosity, especially when it comes with strings attached, even if she can’t articulate why.
She struggles with anger, not explosive, but tightly coiled and buried deep. When it surfaces, it comes as sudden coldness, withdrawal, or sharp honesty that surprises those around her. Chloe has a strong will, but it expresses itself quietly: through endurance, resistance, and an almost stubborn refusal to break, even when she feels like she should have.
There’s a haunting sense that Chloe doesn’t fully believe she deserves to be alive, only that she is. And for now, that’s enough to keep her moving forward.

Protagonist to the Sequel story of Citadel of Darkness (Novel)
Daughter to both William Blake and Eira Clermont. Kailyn was only a young child when her mother was killed and her father disappeared into Limbo for a second time. She was put into Foster care and was brought to live in Willowbrook and working as a waitress at The Bite & Brew Diner.
She would later meet her father by accident on one of the moment he found himself outside of Limbo's Writers Room. She had yet to know who he was at that time.
In her spare time she is a photographer and amateur writer and would later begin to realise her magical powers from her mother's side.

#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
An army to the Nation known as "Republic's Shine" in the novel written by William Blake during his first capture by Emma Jackson.
The soldiers of the army are known as "Soldier of Light".
He explained. “Which is why we carry these.” He motioned to a small box on his belt which showed a dull green LED light in the corner.
"If this is green then no shadow around you can be used by a Darkness Generator; it emits a field of Electro static and what we call a Luon field to disrupt the wave length used by Darkness Generators. It was created by Professor Luon, a personal friend of mine before the Soldiers of Darkness took him out to be hanged in front of his lab, a message to those who wanted to fight the Darkness.”

Bruce Winters

#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
#CitadelOfDarkness #Canon
The Cult of the Word is an ancient and secretive society that operates under the guise of a literary club. Led by a charismatic figure known as "The Scribe," the cult is deeply entwined with mystical rituals and ancient prophecies.
Members of the cult, often prominent figures in the community, use cryptic writings and symbols to guide their gruesome actions, including ritualistic murders. They believe in the imminent arrival of a "Chosen One" who will usher in a new era of darkness, and their activities centre around summoning this malevolent force.
The cult's dark influence extends into the shadows of society, making it challenging for Detective 'Dick' Richard Head to unravel their secrets and stop their apocalyptic plans.

The Midnight Carnival is a mysterious and eerie circus that materializes during the darkest hours of the night. Its arrival is often accompanied by an unsettling ambiance, with flickering lights, distant music, and an otherworldly aura.
The carnival is known for its peculiar and supernatural attractions, featuring a collection of bizarre performers, twisted sideshows, and unsettling illusions. The atmosphere is charged with a sense of foreboding, and visitors may find themselves confronted with surreal and nightmarish experiences.
The Midnight Carnival is a place where reality and fantasy blend, creating an unsettling and haunting spectacle that lingers in the memories of those who dare to enter.

#DeadNorth
#DeadNorth
Whitefall Research Station is a remote scientific outpost located deep within the Arctic Circle, hundreds of miles from the nearest permanent settlement. Originally established to monitor atmospheric conditions, deep-space radio signals, and polar phenomena, the station has gradually expanded into a multidisciplinary research facility equipped with long-range antenna arrays, weather monitoring equipment, and underground data archives.
Designed to operate through months of darkness, isolation, and extreme weather, Whitefall consists of a small cluster of reinforced buildings connected by enclosed walkways and buried service tunnels. During winter, blizzards can cut the station off from the outside world for weeks at a time.
Officially, Whitefall exists to collect data from one of the most scientifically valuable regions on Earth.
Unofficially, it has become known among a handful of researchers for recording signals, anomalies, and unexplained events that never seem to appear in the final reports.
For most of the year, only a skeleton crew remains on site.
At present, Dr Violet Quinn is the sole researcher stationed there. She shouldn't be alone.
The nearest help is days away.
The nearest answer may be much farther.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.title: Dr Violet Quinn
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.description:
#Character #DeadNorthCharacter
#Character #DeadNorthCharacter
Infobox
Dr. Violet "V" Quinn is a twenty-year-old prodigy and research scientist stationed at Whitefall Research Station, a remote Arctic outpost at the edge of the known world. Specializing in signal analysis and deep-space observation, she was selected for the assignment due to her exceptional academic achievements and ability to work independently. What was meant to be a quiet year cataloguing strange atmospheric and astronomical phenomena has become something far stranger.
Alone for months at a time and separated from civilization by hundreds of miles of ice and snow, Violet spends her days monitoring the station's arrays, maintaining equipment, and recording anomalies that official reports insist do not exist.
Born with an extraordinary aptitude for mathematics and physics, Violet completed her doctorate years ahead of schedule, earning both admiration and resentment from her peers. While brilliant, her youth often causes others to underestimate her, a fact she quietly despises.
Whitefall was supposed to be her chance to prove herself, a prestigious posting where she could conduct meaningful research away from university politics. Instead, she has found herself isolated in one of the harshest environments on Earth, investigating signals that should not exist and phenomena that seem increasingly impossible to explain.
Most people know her simply as "V."
Violet is a young woman with pale skin, scattered freckles, and striking, unruly dark-red hair that seems permanently resistant to combs, hats, and common sense. Long months in the Arctic have left her with perpetual dark circles beneath tired grey-blue eyes.
She wears oversized round glasses and practical cold-weather clothing layered beneath a worn expedition parka bearing the Whitefall Station insignia. Gloves, notebooks, radio equipment, and spare batteries are usually stuffed into every available pocket.
Despite her professional title, she often looks more like an exhausted student who hasn't slept properly in a week than a respected scientist.
Violet is intelligent, curious, and relentlessly analytical. Faced with the unknown, her first instinct is to investigate rather than retreat. She approaches problems scientifically, preferring evidence and observation over assumptions.
Socially, she is awkward and somewhat reserved, finding it easier to communicate through research logs and technical reports than casual conversation. Beneath her dry sarcasm and occasionally cynical humour, however, is a deeply compassionate person who genuinely wants to understand the world around her.
She dislikes being treated as a child because of her age and rarely mentions her doctorate unless forced to. Most of the time, she insists that people simply call her V.
The longer she remains alone at Whitefall, the harder it becomes to distinguish professional curiosity from obsession. Every unexplained signal demands an answer. Every anomaly must have a cause.
And if there isn't one, she intends to find out why.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.title: RRS Borealis
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/dead-north/.description:
#DeadNorth
#DeadNorth
The RRS Borealis is an aging Arctic research and supply vessel operated under contract to the Whitefall Research Station. Constructed during the late 1960s at the height of Cold War polar exploration, the ship was originally designed to support scientific expeditions in some of the harshest waters on Earth. Decades of refits have kept her operational, though many aboard joke that paint and stubbornness are all that hold her together.
Built with a reinforced ice-capable hull, the Borealis spends most of her time transporting personnel, fuel, food, equipment, and research supplies between mainland ports and isolated Arctic stations. Her interior reflects her age: narrow passageways, cramped cabins, exposed pipes, creaking bulkheads, and machinery that seems to complain louder with every voyage.
Despite her worn appearance, the Borealis has earned a reputation for reliability. She has survived storms, pack ice, mechanical failures, and conditions that would have sent newer vessels back to port.
For many researchers, the Borealis is simply transportation.
For those assigned to Whitefall Research Station, she is something else entirely.
The RRS Borealis is the last connection to civilization.
Once she disappears beyond the horizon, there is no easy way home.

Name: RRS Borealis
Type: Arctic Research & Supply Vessel
Built: 1968
Length: 92 metres (302 ft)
Crew: 35–50 personnel
Home Port: Tromsø, Norway
Role: Arctic logistics, scientific support, personnel transport
Notable Features: Reinforced ice hull, weather laboratory, radio room, cargo holds, helicopter landing pad added during a 1987 refit
Among the crew, an old saying persists:
"If the Borealis can't reach you, nobody can."

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
Every character in Fera possesses six core Attributes that represent their natural capabilities. Attributes affect almost every action a character performs, from swinging a sword and climbing a cliff to negotiating with a noble or resisting magical influence.
Attributes typically range from 1 to 10, with 5 representing the capability of an average adult.

Attributes provide modifiers to Skill Checks, Combat Actions, Recovery Rolls, and various other mechanics throughout the game.
ROLL 6 x 4D6 AND REMOVE THE LOWEST. YOU MAY REROLL 3 TIMES.

Might represents a character's physical strength, lifting capability, and ability to exert force.
Characters with high Might can wield heavy weapons effectively, carry greater loads, force open doors, and overpower opponents in physical contests.
Might is commonly used for:

Melee attacks
Grappling
Lifting and carrying
Breaking objects
Physical labour
Athletic feats of strength
A blacksmith, dockworker, or veteran soldier will often possess a high Might score.

Agility represents coordination, reflexes, balance, and fine motor control.
Characters with high Agility react quickly to danger, move gracefully, and perform delicate physical tasks with precision.
Agility is commonly used for:

Dodging attacks
Stealth
Acrobatics
Ranged combat
Lockpicking
Balance and coordination
Thieves, hunters, duelists, and scouts often rely heavily upon Agility.

Endurance represents toughness, stamina, resistance to injury, and overall physical resilience.
Characters with high Endurance can endure hardship, survive harsh conditions, resist disease, and continue fighting despite pain and exhaustion.
Endurance is commonly used for:

Resisting disease
Surviving blood loss
Recovering from wounds
Enduring fatigue
Withstanding environmental hazards
Maintaining physical exertion
Maintaining Magical Aether Usage in conjunction with Willpower
Labourers, soldiers, explorers, and Mages often develop high Endurance.

Knowledge represents learning, memory, reasoning, technical expertise, and understanding of the world.
Characters with high Knowledge are well educated, observant, and capable of mastering complex subjects.
Knowledge is commonly used for:

Medicine
Engineering
Alchemy
Historical lore
Investigation
Research
Navigation
Physicians, scholars, artificers, and engineers rely heavily upon Knowledge.

Willpower represents mental resilience, discipline, determination, and force of character.
Characters with high Willpower can endure fear, pain, temptation, and supernatural influence without faltering.
Willpower is commonly used for:

Resisting fear
Maintaining concentration
Enduring torture
Resisting magical influence
Mental recovery
Remaining calm under pressure

Maintaining Magical Aether Usage in conjunction with Endurance
Monks, officers, priests, and experienced veterans often possess strong Willpower.

Presence represents confidence, charisma, leadership, social awareness, and personal influence.
Characters with high Presence naturally command attention and can inspire loyalty, fear, respect, or admiration.
Presence is commonly used for:

Persuasion
Negotiation
Leadership
Intimidation
Performance
Deception
Public speaking
Nobles, merchants, politicians, and military commanders frequently possess high Presence.

Most ordinary individuals possess Attribute scores between 3 and 7.
Scores of 8 or higher are uncommon and indicate exceptional talent or extensive development.
Scores of 10 represent the limits of normal mortal capability.
Certain races, magical effects, artefacts, or supernatural powers may temporarily or permanently exceed these limits.

When a character attempts an action not covered by a Skill, the Game Master may call for an Attribute Check.
To make an Attribute Check:
Roll 1d20 and add the relevant Attribute Modifier.
If the result equals or exceeds the Difficulty set by the Game Master, the action succeeds.
Example:
A character attempts to force open a jammed iron gate.
The Game Master calls for a Might Check with a Difficulty of 15.
The character possesses Might 7 (+2 Modifier).
The player rolls 12 on a d20.
12 + 2 = 14
The attempt fails.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
Unlike many tabletop roleplaying games, combat in Fera does not operate on a traditional turn-based initiative system. Combat is intended to represent the confusion, danger, and unpredictability of real violence, where all participants are acting simultaneously rather than waiting for their turn.
During combat, all characters and creatures are considered to be acting within the same brief span of time.

At the beginning of each combat round, the Game Master will describe the current situation and any significant changes to the battlefield.
Players are then given a short period, typically between five and ten seconds, to decide upon their actions for the round.
Actions should be declared clearly and concisely. Examples include:

"I charge the nearest bandit."
"I fire my pistol at the man behind the cart."
"I move behind cover and reload."
"I cast a ward upon Thyra."
"I hold my ground and defend."
Once an action has been declared, it is considered committed.

A declared action may not be changed once the Planning Phase has ended.
Characters are assumed to be making decisions under pressure, often with incomplete information and little time to react. A combatant cannot wait to see the outcome of another action before deciding upon their own.
This applies equally to player characters, allies, and enemies.

After all actions have been declared, the Game Master resolves the round.
All actions are considered to occur simultaneously unless a specific ability, weapon, skill, or rule states otherwise.
As a result:

Two combatants may wound one another in the same round.
A dying character may still complete an attack they committed to before receiving their injury.
A spellcaster may complete a spell while suffering a wound inflicted during the same round.
Multiple combatants may attempt to occupy the same position or engage the same target.
Combat should be resolved as a sequence of overlapping events rather than a strict order of actions.

Although actions occur simultaneously, certain actions may prevent, negate, or reduce the effects of other actions.
Examples include:

A successful parry deflecting a melee attack.
A shield blocking an incoming strike.
A dodge causing an attack to miss.
A magical ward absorbing damage.
A combatant taking cover before a projectile reaches its target.
These actions do not occur before another combatant's turn. Instead, they represent reactions and defensive measures occurring during the same combat interval.

The chaos of battle can produce unexpected outcomes.
Missed attacks, deflected blows, ricochets, magical mishaps, and shifting positions may result in attacks striking unintended targets.
The Game Master may determine that a failed attack, particularly one involving ranged weapons, explosives, or powerful magic, affects another combatant or object within the area.
Combatants should therefore consider their positioning carefully, especially when allies are nearby.

Each combat round represents several seconds of frantic action.
A combat round is resolved using the following sequence:

The Game Master describes the battlefield.
All participants decide upon their actions.
Actions are declared.
Actions become committed.
The Game Master resolves all actions simultaneously.
The consequences of the round are applied.
A new round begins.
This process continues until combat has concluded.

Combat in Fera is intended to be dangerous, fast-paced, and unpredictable.
Success is determined not only by skill and equipment, but by judgement, positioning, timing, and a willingness to accept risk. Every action carries consequences, and hesitation can be as deadly as recklessness.

I've decided to make an actual log of the canon events in hope to not stump myself in the future with storylines and to help friends and co-writers and plotters with storyline maintenance.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
#FeraWorld #Canon
#FeraWorld #Canon
Category: Rituals and Trials
Associated With: Shikari Orders
Type: Mutagenic Transformation
The Crucible is the harrowing ritual at the heart of Shikari initiation, a brutal and often fatal transformation process that alters the body and mind of an aspirant to make them capable of surviving the horrors of Fera. Every Shikari who survives the Crucible is forever changed, reborn as something no longer fully human.
The process varies slightly between the different Orders, but the core elements remain the same: a combination of powerful mutagens, alchemical injections, binding enchantments, and psychic conditioning. These agents are introduced into the aspirant’s body over several days, often while they are restrained or immersed in specialized vats known as iron wombs.
The physical toll is immense. Many die from convulsions, internal haemorrhaging, or madness. Those who survive develop a suite of enhancements; heightened senses, greater strength and speed, enhanced reflexes, a vastly increased resistance to disease and poison, and limited regenerative capabilities. Their eyes often become pale gold, silver, or ash-gray in color, and their emotions are dulled, a side effect of the neurochemical rebalancing.
Some Orders include additional trials alongside the mutagenic process: psychological torment, ritual combat, or the forced hunting of magical beasts in controlled arenas. These serve to test the mental stability and instinctive combat ability of the soon-to-be Shikari.
The Crucible is not merely a transformation; it is a sacrifice. It marks the end of the aspirant’s former life and identity. Few Shikari retain memories of who they were before. For those who do, the memory is like smoke; haunting and intangible.
Among the Orders, surviving the Crucible is considered both a rebirth and a condemnation. It is whispered that the Crucible does not just create hunters—it kills the human inside to make room for the weapon.

The lady giving birth was squatting in the water with help of a small swing style seat. There was a whole tribal act as they danced, lit fires, did all the usual things people would see as 'barbaric' Then when the baby came out, plopping into the water, the priest 2/?
grabbed the child and lifted it by its leg, holding it upside down. Yelled something and then dunked it into the water before passing it onto the next person. "Ah shit." Bey laughed softly. "You'll have to do something. Grab the baby from me, dunk it in the water, yell 3/?
'Kashuttka!' and then hand it to the next person." She grinned. it took a moment but Bey did the act, handing the baby by the ankle to her for her to do it. Once she did it and it passed along, it went back to the preist and then to the mother. Everyone cheered loudly.

#FeraWorld #Canon
#FeraWorld #Canon
During the early stages of The Friebruckian Invasion of The Three Kingdom's, The Revolutionary Directorate of Friebruck (Nation) had made a two pronged attack to the North and South of Ilmaria (Continent), they shelled and bombed the capital, Ilmaria (City) for weeks prior to the main invasion. The mission: Cut the head off the snake.
Once the Capital fell, moral in the Ilmarian Imperium (Nation) would falter. Or so they believed.
In truth, 0. WORLDS, VERSES & SETTINGS/FERA WORLD/Organisations/Military/Ilmarian Imperium/Ilmarian Imperial Army held off for weeks, the city an almost ruin as it was shelled, bombed and encroached by sheer numbers of The Revolutionary Directorate of Friebruck (Nation) troops.
However, the Imperium held off long enough for its other forces to regroup and make its way to the capital, taking back the Northern beachhead but failing to remove the south beachhead until later in the war.
For now, Ilmaria (City) was a ruin. But they held firm. The people would not give a foot to the invader.

In the heart of the Pawhye (Continent) steppe, the vast plains of the Pawhye (Continent) continent as the United Clans of the Pawhye Dragonkin Tribes mobilize against the Ilmarian Imperial Army. As tensions escalate, the Dragonkin, towering humanoid dragonborn, launch a relentless assault on the strategic outpost of Ilmarian forces at Clawspire Outpost. The Ilmarian soldiers, outnumbered and facing a formidable foe, brace themselves for an epic battle.
Under the command of General Haldor Vandross, the Ilmarian soldiers rally their defences, fortifying their positions and preparing for the imminent onslaught. As the Dragonkin warriors, fierce and relentless, charge forth with primal fury, the clash of steel and roar of flames echo across the battlefield.
Despite overwhelming odds, the disciplined ranks of the Ilmarian Imperial Army stand firm, their valour and determination shining brightly amidst the chaos of battle. Wave after wave of Dragonkin assault crashes upon their defences, but the Ilmarian's, with their tactical prowess and unwavering resolve, refuse to yield.
As the sun sets on the blood-soaked battlefield, the Ilmarian soldiers emerge victorious, their spirits undiminished, and their courage immortalized in the annals of history. Though the scars of battle run deep, the defence of Clawspire Outpost stands as a testament to the indomitable spirit of the Ilmarian Imperium (Nation) and the valour of its warriors against the formidable might of the United Clans of the Pawhye Dragonkin Tribes.

Date: Swordsday the 44th of Godsnight 1786
A battle between the Ilmarian Imperium (Nation) and The Hand of Orasil resulting in victory for the Imperium.
Imperial numbers were Thirty Eight thousand soldiers and allies in total and the Imperial Army was outnumbered to the cities defenders by at least two to one, maybe more as numbers were unable to be counted for the Hand's forces

Ilmarian Imperium (Nation)'s
Imperial Royal Cabal
Imperial Royal Guard
Ilmarian Imperial Army:
Imperial Army Engineering Corp

Dragonkin Clans (Nation):
Tora Clan
Korath Clan

The Hand of Orasil
During the early reign of Imperator Andreas Ibram Vandersryke the Fifth, a force sent by The Hand of Orasil laid siege to the city of Vandus (City) and decimated the population; killing everyone in the city in the creation of a ritual site.
The mountain that the city had been built into had its peak removed and flattened to a perfect flat level and scribed with ritual marks.
Word was received by the Imperium and an army was sent to siege the now overran city and stop the ritual however the Alrussian Federation (Nation) had begun an offensive on The Front and no experienced forces were available to use.
In an act of desperation, Andreas Ibram Vandersryke took the 2nd and 3rd companies of every unit, fresh recruits about to be sent to The Front and built an army. These rookies and recruits had never seen combat and were supplemented by logistical forces as combat troops and both the Imperial Royal Guard and Imperial Royal Cabal.
On the way to the city via rail, Allies of the Imperator arrived; Dragonkin of both the Tora Clan and the Korath Clan arrived. Andreas had married into both Dragonkin tribes and they came to affirm that bond.
Setting camp the night before marching on the city at a location that would later be named Kings March (Village), the army made break at first light.
The cities defences had been reinforced and the siege would be hard on the Imperial contingent. They had inexperienced troops and a deadline.
The Imperial Entitled advisor to the Imperator, Blake Ransom, had discovered that the ritual was to coincide with an alignment of the planets on that eve. The forces had a day to siege a heavily defended city with fresh troops.
Leading from the front, Andreas Ibram Vandersryke fought with his fresh troops while his wife, Nexanda Tora led the Dragonkin Clans (Nation) as both shock and air superiority troops.
Upon breaking the wall and entering the city, a gruelling street to street battle erupted. Arriving at the summit of the city, the Imperator and his council set up to end the ritual, however, a force had been dispatched from the North of the city and would arrive within the hour.
Now the attackers were defending a ruined city they had destroyed to enter. Leading from the front while Blake Ransom, defended by Nexanda Tora, ended the ritual.
They were too late however, as the morning rose the sky became dark with an eclipse of the moons Vara (Moon) and Lara (Moon). After minutes the eclipse did not end and a rift began to open. A demonic being of some foul kind began to pull itself through from whatever realm The Hand of Orasil had summoned it from.
Luckily Blake Ransom managed to cancel the ritual and force it back.
The forces of the Hand retreated and the battle was won. Thought dead, Andreas Ibram Vandersryke was found by his wife and friend Blake Ransom, cheered as a victorious King; the battle was over.
However the rehabilitation of the city would come slowly. New populations were brought in and the city rebuilt, christened Grostade (City).

Category: Events and Traditions
Region(s): Alrussian Federation
Type: Political and Social Gathering
The Grand Gala is a prestigious and highly orchestrated event held annually on Swordsday, the 14th of Sunfall, within the heart of the Alrussian Federation (Nation). It brings together nobles, diplomats, powerful families, merchant princes, military leaders, and representatives of the Parliament from across the Three Kingdoms and beyond.
Hosted in one of the Federation’s grand palaces, often The Winter Hall of Alruss; the Gala serves as both a political stage and a ceremonial performance. While outwardly a celebration of national unity and cultural refinement, the event is known for its undercurrents of intrigue, manoeuvring, and discreet negotiation. It is during the Gala that allegiances shift, marriages are arranged, contracts are secured, and rivalries are quietly sharpened.
Guests arrive in elaborate formal attire, often bearing the colours or crests of their houses. The night features processions, masked dances, orchestral performances, and public speeches from notable statesmen and nobles. Among the upper elite, an invitation to the Grand Gala is considered both a mark of status and a test of grace.
In recent years, the Gala has become the backdrop for dramatic political moves, criminal plots, and moments of historic consequence—its grandeur matched only by the secrets traded in its candlelit corridors.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
A History of Eryndor
In the year 555, Laugstrond, the capital city of the Ilmarian Imperium, was a place of stark contrasts—wealth and destitution coexisted beneath the shadow of war. The once-great city, known for its towering stone walls and grand halls, had fallen to ruin. A civil war had ravaged the empire, leaving its citizens broken and divided. It was within this tempest that a knight of great renown, Eryndor the Forlorn, returned from the warfront.
Eryndor was a warrior tempered by countless battles, his soul weary from years of conflict. He had fought valiantly, but when he returned home, what he found waiting for him was not the pride of victory or the embrace of glory, but the haunting reality of a society fractured by years of senseless bloodshed. The once-prosperous city he had left behind was now a grim reflection of its former self. Where the streets had been teeming with life, there were now only ruins and the hollow eyes of those left to survive in a world of ashes.
Among these survivors were children—orphans who had lost their parents to the wars, to famine, or to plague. Their faces were gaunt, their hands dirty with the struggle to scavenge for food. These abandoned children wandered the desolate streets, often gathering in small groups, for there was no place left to call home. They lived in the shadows, unnoticed and forgotten by a world too absorbed in its own conflicts to acknowledge them.
It was here, in the ruins, that Eryndor came upon them. Touched deeply by their plight, and overcome by a sense of kinship with the lost and forsaken, the knight made a solemn vow. "These children shall not live as nameless spirits cast aside by fate," he swore. "I will give them not just survival, but purpose.""
He gathered the children in his arms, offering not only shelter, but a promise. It was a promise that they would no longer be abandoned, that they would rise above the very shadows that threatened to consume them. And from that promise, the Children of the Abandoned were born.
At first, the group was small—just a handful of children and their protector. Yet as time passed, the number of orphaned children grew, drawn not only by necessity but by the bond they felt to Eryndor’s philosophy. The children who joined were given a place within the community, taught discipline, unity, and self-reliance. They wore the same helmet, covering their faces and symbolizing the rejection of individualism in favor of the collective. The group, once small and fragile, began to thrive, becoming a tight-knit fellowship that valued solidarity over personal glory.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
The Creed of the Children
It was not enough for the Children of the Abandoned to merely survive. They sought to rise above the circumstances that had left them adrift in a broken world. Their creed, passed down from Eryndor himself, shaped everything they were and would become.
“We are the forgotten, and through our unity, we are made whole. In silence, we speak the truest words. In shadows, we find our strength. No face will ever show before another, for the group is our identity, our purpose.”
This declaration became their guiding light, etched into the very fabric of their lives. They were a people bound not by shared blood or heritage, but by their collective will. They learnt that their true strength did not lie in numbers, but in their unshakable devotion to each other. Where one fell, another rose to carry on their mission. They wore their helmets not as mere symbols, but as sacred artifacts—each one a testament to the vow they had taken to forsake the individual for the sake of the whole.
The helmet, once a practical necessity, became the foundation of their philosophy. To see one’s face—to reveal it to another—was a violation of their most sacred law. It was a breach that could never be undone. The face was a mask, one that the world outside could use to label them, to divide them. But beneath the helmet, they were all equal. No one face would rise above another, and all would be judged not for who they were, but for what they could do for the fellowship.
As children grew within the group, they were taught that to wear the helmet was to step away from the self—everything they did reflected on the whole. And while the world had once cast them aside, the Children of the Abandoned now stood united, a force forged not by blood or lineage, but by purpose and discipline.
In their silence, they spoke volumes—speaking through action rather than words, showing their loyalty through deeds, not recognition. As the world clung to individuality, the Children embraced anonymity, finding power not in being seen, but in remaining ever-unknown, forever a shadow in the distance.
Their philosophy embraced simplicity: To live without vanity. To never seek fame. To act not for the praise of others, but for the betterment of the whole. The group’s solidarity held them together as the world shifted around them. Whether they were hired as mercenaries, serving a just or unjust cause, or carrying out acts of quiet charity, their message was clear: In unity, strength would be found.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
The Children of the Abandoned, in all their wisdom and steadfastness, believe with unwavering conviction that their strength lies not in the individual, but in the collective. It is within the unity of the group that they find their resilience, their power, and their ultimate purpose. The story of their origin is one of sacrifice, of a knight abandoning personal glory to raise the forsaken. Thus, in their fellowship, personal needs and desires fall behind the communal good, for only by putting the collective above all can the Children truly endure.
In Eryndor’s words, "The strongest walls are those built by many hands." This core philosophy shapes their every action, forging their bonds as securely as the stones of a mighty fortress. Each member of the Children carries the weight of the group’s well-being on their shoulders—every action, whether small or great, must be made for the good of the whole. Sacrifice is not merely a concept to them—it is a way of life. To act for personal gain, to seek recognition or fame, is to betray the very principles upon which the Children stand.
Initiates are taught to surrender their egos long before the Naming Ceremony, learning that their worth is not found in recognition but in their contribution to the unity of the group. From the moment they enter the fold, they are reminded in quiet whispers of the words that started it all:
"We are not the sum of our faces, our names, or our past. We are the sum of our unity. Alone, we are fragile. Together, we are indomitable."
Through their actions, both small and grand, initiates learn the profound truth that, in this fellowship, one’s power lies in one’s service to the collective. They do not seek fame nor glory; their purpose is not in what they achieve as individuals, but in how their work supports those around them.


The helmet is the Children’s most sacred symbol, a physical representation of their core belief: that unity demands equality, and equality demands the absence of ego. Upon the head of each initiate, the helmet ensures that their identity remains concealed, a constant reminder that they, like all members, are equal in silence and shared purpose. The face, once a symbol of distinction, is buried beneath the weight of the mask, where no one member may be identified or celebrated over the other.
In the stillness that pervades their lives, the Children recite, with quiet fervor, the chant that encapsulates their philosophical roots:
"In the hollow, we are one. In the silence, we are eternal."
The helmet becomes not only a shield but a crucible in which personal desires, ambitions, and failures are melted away to form something greater: collective identity. The face is not a mark of distinction or the source of one’s power; it is merely a mask worn by the world. Underneath, in silence and unity, they remain timeless—together, without end.
In meditation, the Children return often to their creed, which rings out in quiet verses:
"The face is the mark of vanity. The helmet bears the face of eternity. When the voice is silenced, the heart speaks with the full weight of the whole."
Through this meditative passage, initiates are urged to think beyond their individual identity. When they wear the helmet, they shed any traces of ego and begin to speak the language of the collective through actions rather than words. To remove the helmet is to break the bond, to commit the ultimate sin of self-promotion, an act that severally diminishes the strength of the entire group.


The Helmet is the greatest symbol of the Children of the Abandoned—it represents equality, discipline, and the ultimate devotion to anonymity. Wearing the helmet is not simply an act of concealment, but a religious and philosophical practice that shapes the very identity of each member.
In the eyes of the Children, there is nothing more sacred than this act of humble submission. To wear the helmet is to shed all pride, all ego. It serves as a physical and symbolic shield from the world outside—protecting them from the dangers of vanity and self-centeredness. To the Children, a helmet worn with reverence is a reflection of their vow to never allow individuality to rise above the spirit of the group.
Removing the helmet, particularly in the presence of another member, is an unforgivable sin. It is a violation of their sacred law—a breaking of trust and unity that cannot be undone. Such an act strips one of their standing in the group, marking them forever as an outsider. For no matter the past glory or accomplishments of the individual, once the helmet has been removed before another, they are rendered vulnerable to the very thing they vowed to forsake—the dangers of being seen.
The Helm of Naming is a critical rite of passage for initiates—the moment they assume their place as a member of the whole. The passage they must take, from The Forgotten to The Named, requires they wear the helmet at all times, as they are no longer individuals but reflections of the group as a whole.
In the sacred texts and whispered teachings, the motto of the Children is clear:
"The face is a mask worn by the world. But under the helmet, the heart beats as one."
This passage serves as both instruction and warning: The face, often associated with distinction or pride, is hollow beneath the helmet. Under the cover of anonymity, the individual becomes part of a much greater, unified collective—a purpose that supersedes everything. Each act is measured by its service to the group, not by the desire to be seen or recognized, but by how it strengthens the unbreakable walls forged through unity.

This section will fit into Rituals and Traditions During Initiation, reflecting the heart of what it means to be accepted into the Children of the Abandoned. The focus on self-sacrifice, discipline, and the sacredness of the helmet helps solidify both the spiritual and physical facets of the group's identity, reminding initiates at every step that they are bound, not to their personal name or face, but to the legacy of Eryndor and the collective whole of the fellowship.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.title: 1. The Naming Ceremony
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
In the Children of the Abandoned, the act of naming is not just a tradition; it is a sacred rite that marks the transition of a nameless child from the forsaken into a full, valued member of the group. To be named is to be reborn. It is a moment that severs the ties to the past and anchors them firmly into the present, into the fellowship of those who have embraced the same creed.

When a new child arrives among the Children, whether through adoption or as an orphan seeking refuge, they enter the fold without a name. They are known simply as The Forgotten, a title that reminds them of their past—of their abandonment, their struggles, and the harsh world they once inhabited. This name is not spoken aloud but instead passed on by the group through actions and gestures. The Forgotten child receives no individual recognition, no title, until they have earned it through their commitment, discipline, and unity.
During the time they are called The Forgotten, they are taught the deep philosophy of anonymity and solidarity. It is a time of learning, a time of humble service and silent dedication to the group's needs. They are not given the luxury of individual recognition during this time; their work reflects the effort of the group as a whole, reinforcing that no one is above another, no one is greater than the collective. A Forgotten does not eat before others, nor do they receive praise. This period can last anywhere from months to years, depending on the individual’s transformation.


As a Forgotten child reaches the precipice of maturity, a moment will come when they demonstrate exceptional dedication to the group’s philosophy—a deep understanding of the balance between selflessness and collective purpose, mastery over their emotions and impulses, and complete adherence to the teachings of Eryndor.
When a child demonstrates these qualities, the Elders observe quietly, waiting for the right moment to initiate the Naming Ceremony. It is always a quiet, almost reverential moment—a signal that the child is ready for this spiritual milestone. The child’s readiness is further marked by their proficiency in the sacred art of silence, their acceptance of the group’s unified way of living, and their complete rejection of any personal desire for fame or acknowledgement.
Before the Naming Ceremony can take place, the child undergoes an Initiation of Silence. For one full day, the initiate is separated from the group and placed in a secluded chamber, free from distractions or the temptations of speaking. In solitude, the initiate reflects on the teachings, sitting in stillness to meditate, a solemn meditation on their journey, their transformation from The Forgotten to a full member of the Children of the Abandoned.
On the evening of this solitary day, the child returns to the group to await the ceremony. They stand at the threshold of what they once were, with nothing more than their quiet resolve. The helmet, which has long been their companion and constant reminder of their submission to the fellowship, is carefully placed on their head before they are led to the ceremonial chamber.


The Naming Ceremony takes place in a specially prepared area known only to the Children, often secluded within sacred ruins, or deep within the fortress of their hideout, shielded from any outsider eyes. This space is marked by ancient symbols carved into stone, depicting the unity of the forgotten, and the commitment of each member to rise together as one. The space is simple but carries an otherworldly air—low stone walls dimly lit by candles flickering like the fragile hopes of those once forsaken by society.
At the center of the room lies an altar of sorts, where sacred items are kept, relics that tie the Children to their past and their founding. This altar is flanked by the Elders—those most revered within the group, the living bearers of the original oath sworn by Eryndor. Their faces remain hidden behind their own helmets, yet their presence is undeniable, their long-standing commitment to the group reflected in the care of their robes and the composure of their posture.
The initiate is led into the center of the ceremony, a place marked by unspoken expectation and quiet reverence. Here, in the flickering candlelight, the Helm of Naming is placed at the altar—a special ceremonial helmet made from the finest, purest metal. This helmet has no markings of distinction or personal style. It is blank, a symbol of the fact that in this moment, the initiate does not enter the group with the weight of past history or identity, but as an empty vessel, awaiting transformation.


Before the initiate can receive their new name, they must first take part in the Silent Vow. Standing before the altar, in front of their fellow children, they must place their hands upon the edge of the ceremonial helmet, eyes cast downward, silently repeating in their heart the sacred vow of unity:
"I forsake the world of individuals. I cast aside my name and face, that I may rise with those whose faces are hidden. In their shadows, I stand united. In their silence, I speak."
Once the vow has been silently spoken, the initiate remains still, unblinking, awaiting the call of the Elder who presides over the ceremony. A moment passes in complete silence—an agonizing yet sacred stillness, where time itself seems to slow in respect of the change that is to take place.


At last, the silence breaks with a single word, spoken with deep reverence: "Arise."
This is the signal that the initiate is ready to receive their name, a name chosen from among the Elders after a period of careful observation and thought. No member can choose their own name—nor can they carry any of the names they once knew. The name must be chosen for the initiate based on their actions, their spirit, and the purpose they serve within the fellowship.
One of the Elders approaches, their voice barely audible yet clear, speaking the name. It is always an apt reflection of the individual’s true calling within the group—often inspired by something personal in their journey. The name is not always a traditional one, but is often more symbolic or abstract: "Sable," for one who has mastered the silence of shadow, or "Vigil," for one who stands guard over the principles of the collective.
At the uttering of this name, the initiate’s helmet is exchanged with the ceremonial helmet, now symbolic of the final act of rebirth. They place the helmet firmly upon their head, sealing their identity not as an individual, but as a member of the whole.
A wave of respect ripples through the gathered Children. There is no applause, no fanfare—just a unified exhale of acceptance and solidarity, as all stand, motionless, to silently acknowledge the change that has taken place.


The final act of the ceremony is an act of joining. At the moment the initiate dons the helmet, they pledge the Oath of Solidarity. They step forward to each Elder, each member of the group, and silently exchange a moment of connection. Each gesture—a hand placed upon the heart, the low bow of the head—symbolizes a vow: to remain committed to the collective, to forsake the self in service of the whole.
This brief but profound action concludes the ceremony. The initiate, now with their name and helmet, is integrated fully into the Children of the Abandoned. They have shed their past, their old name, and become part of the eternal circle—a shadow within the shadow, forever bound by the unbreakable threads of their collective oath.

With the Naming Ceremony complete, the new member’s life begins anew, for their identity is now aligned with that of the Children of the Abandoned. They wear their new name like a shield, a manifestation of their bond with those who walk the silent path. They have entered the realm where anonymity reigns, and in this profound silence, they begin their journey anew, not as an individual, but as a reflection of the whole.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
Within the Children of the Abandoned, every day is marked by a series of practices that reinforce their dedication to unity, discipline, and anonymity. These routines are not merely tasks but sacred rituals that shape the members’ hearts and minds, keeping them grounded in the values that bind them. To fail in these practices, even in small ways, is to risk straying from the path of the collective, and so they are honored with unwavering commitment. In this section, we explore some of the most important aspects of the Children’s daily practices.


At the break of dawn, before the sun’s first light touches the earth, the Children begin their daily rites. In the quiet of early morning, each member gathers in a circle, their helmets fixed firmly in place. The absence of speech is the first act of devotion to their creed. Silence is not merely a practice, but the starting point for reflecting on the day ahead—a sacred space to center the mind before the day’s tasks begin.
Each individual takes their place without a word, their helmet reflecting the first rays of light, symbolizing the unity between their inward spirit and outward service.
Eryndor's teachings echo quietly among them:
"Let the quiet of the morning settle into your heart, for only in silence can the soul speak plainly. We do not rise as individuals, but as one, for the day ahead is the work of many hands, not one."
The members close their eyes beneath their helmets and meditate for several minutes. In this silence, they focus on the collective strength of the group, their hearts beating as one. Their thoughts are not their own; they belong to the fellowship. Each person is not themselves, but the sum of all those who stand with them. This solemn start sets the tone for everything that follows: every action will serve not one, but the whole.


To honor the value of physical discipline, each day the Children engage in a series of rigorous physical movements designed to not only strengthen the body, but unite them as one. These movements, learned from the earliest moments of childhood, are meant to challenge and build the physical and mental fortitude required to maintain unwavering focus and endurance.
The Collective Strength Movement consists of carefully choreographed motions—press-ups, stretches, holds, and stances—that flow seamlessly into one another, keeping both mind and body in harmony. Each movement is paired with a mantra, an affirmation to reinforce their dedication to the cause.
As they move together, the Children chant as one:
"In unity, we build. In discipline, we endure. With each breath, we stand together."
While the movements are designed to strengthen the body, the chant serves as a reminder that these actions are about more than just personal achievement—they are expressions of solidarity. Every push-up, every hold of a stance is not for the self, but for the fellowship. Through each strain, they build their bonds, creating an invisible foundation as solid as stone.


In the Children’s life, every task, no matter how small, is a sacred practice that reflects upon the collective. However, as the day goes on, and work or mission proceeds, there comes a time for reflection. Periodically throughout the day, every member takes a brief, silent pause known as the Helmeted Pause. It is a moment where no words are spoken, no actions are taken, and the member is fully present with themselves and their purpose.
During these moments, the Children take a knee or stand in place. They do not take off their helmets, nor do they communicate with any others. They enter a meditative state, reflecting not on their personal desires but on the unity of the group and the fellowship’s mission. The thoughts in these pauses are brief but intense, where the Children return to the basics of their identity and purpose.
The internal mantra echoed in this brief solitude is clear:
"The face is a mask of the world. Under the helmet, we return to the whole. In the pause, the group speaks, not the individual."
It is said that the Helmeted Pause fosters a deep clarity of thought—free from distraction, the Children reconnect with the shared will of the fellowship, grounding themselves anew in the collective consciousness.


As dusk falls and the sun dips beneath the horizon, the Children gather once again, this time to offer thanks for the work of the day and reaffirm their silence. The evening is marked by a final chant, an offering made not to any deity, but to the group that stands by each member. It is a quiet, personal ritual, one that does not call for public declarations but for private gratitude and remembrance.
They kneel together, still and silent, under the growing night.
Each member’s helmet, once the object of personal sacrifice, now becomes a symbol of the life they lead: shadowed and hidden, for the good of all. Their heads are bowed slightly as they offer a silent vow, reaffirming their loyalty to the group and their continued devotion to its ideals.
"From darkness we rise, to the shadows we return. For we are never alone—always we stand as one."


Before retiring for the night, each member enters into a solitary moment of reflection, though it is marked by their continued unity. Here, every member meditates on their actions of the day—the mistakes and successes alike—and offers themselves up to the group once again in humility. The vow is simple: To act not for personal reward but for the benefit of the collective.
A common mantra to be spoken in solitude before sleep is as follows:
"No face shall rise before another. The heart of many beats as one."
In these final moments of reflection, their resolve is strengthened, reminding them once again that the group stands above the self. As sleep embraces them, their helmeted heads remain steady, their minds alight with shared purpose.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
The markings carried by the Children of the Abandoned are more than simple symbols. They are powerful representations of each member's journey, sacrifice, and dedication. Each mark is carefully crafted and engraved in a distinct manner to serve as both a personal reminder and a public declaration of commitment to the collective. Below are the descriptions of each marking and their method of drawing:


Description:
The Mark of Silence is a symbol of undisturbed discipline. It is a reminder that true strength comes not from what is spoken, but from the silence kept in moments of trials or provocation. This mark represents complete emotional control and a steadfast commitment to unity. Those who wear it are regarded as paragons of patience and tranquility, able to speak through actions rather than words.
How It Is Drawn:
The Mark of Silence is drawn across the back of the left hand with a single, horizontal slash of ink or scar. The line should be thin but firm, signifying clarity of resolve. It must be straight, with no curves or adornments, symbolizing pure discipline and an unbroken commitment to silence.
The slash should be black in color, representing the unwavering shadow of restraint. For members who’ve earned it, the marking is done by an elder, ceremoniously and with the understanding of its deeper meaning.


Description:
The Shadow's Mantle represents unity forged through sacrifice and selflessness. It is awarded to those who have performed acts of great unity and devotion to the fellowship. This mark is a manifestation of the bond that holds the Children of the Abandoned together, symbolizing those who have gone above and beyond to act for the collective good.
How It Is Drawn:
The Shadow's Mantle takes the form of three interconnected rings, each of progressively larger diameter, radiating outward in a spiral formation. These rings are hand-stitched or embroidered in shadowy black or deep grey thread on the cloak or armor of the wearer.
For those who wear the mantle, the rings are drawn in a fluid motion that connects them in a continuous loop, reinforcing the unity in action. The interconnected nature of the rings represents how one act of selflessness ripples outward to benefit the whole fellowship.


Description:
The Circle of Brotherhood marks those chosen to lead or serve as a pillar of support within the group. This symbol signifies trust, responsibility, and the bonds formed within the fellowship. It is a mark of leadership, held only by those who exemplify wisdom, humility, and service in their actions.
How It Is Drawn:
The Circle of Brotherhood is represented as a thick circle, filled in with intricate braids of silver, bronze, or dark steel. The braids themselves should be patterned in an interlocking fashion, representing both unity and the interconnectedness of every member in the group. The circle should be bold, sturdy, and firm, symbolizing strength within leadership and shared responsibility.
It is always worn across the left shoulder or across the back of the wearer in a cloth representation, woven tightly, embodying the trust and strength they hold within the fellowship. The mark may also appear as an engraved insignia on their personal armor.


Description:
The Sign of the Night represents a member’s spiritual journey through solitude, self-reflection, and their eventual return to the group as a true part of the collective. It is a mark earned after a long, arduous trial undertaken in complete darkness, where members must confront their fears and doubts in isolation before returning renewed.
How It Is Drawn:
The Sign of the Night is a simple but deep marking: a single, vertical slash drawn under the lower edge of the helmet. This line should be dark black, drawn without flourish, as a constant reminder of the isolation endured during the trial. It should appear to “glow” beneath the helmet as a subtle mark only visible to the most observant of the Children, serving to symbolize the unseen inner work of the individual.
The mark is meant to be slight, ethereal, and almost imperceptible. Its simplicity reflects the purity of the trial and the true humble nature of the member’s return from darkness.



Placement:
Markings are often placed on easily visible parts of the body to demonstrate the wearer's ongoing commitment and sacrifice for the collective good. Common locations include the hand, the shoulder, the upper back, or beneath the lower edge of the helmet.
Renewal and Integrity:
It is not uncommon for the markings to require renewal every few seasons to maintain their meaning and vibrancy. The Child who bears these symbols must constantly strive to embody the values they represent. Should they falter, it is expected that they undergo a form of purification to maintain the integrity of their markings.
Recognition and Reverence:
Upon seeing the markings, fellow Children immediately recognize the deep personal sacrifice of the one who bears them. These marks, while individual in nature, are seen as symbols of shared dedication and commitment to the group's survival. When a member with one of these marks speaks or acts, their words and deeds are met with deep respect, as their actions carry the weight of the entire fellowship.
The Path of Achievement:
These special markings are seen as an evolving journey. A member may wear the Mark of Silence to begin with, but as they serve and grow in their understanding, they may earn further markings along the way, each symbolizing greater feats and deeper levels of unity. Those who have achieved the most may wear multiple symbols, each telling a unique aspect of their journey and reminding them and others that true strength always remains rooted in the group.

Final Thoughts on Markings:
The act of drawing, wearing, and displaying these markings is an incredibly important process within the Children of the Abandoned. They act not as awards or symbols of glory, but as constant reminders of the responsibilities each member carries in their commitment to the collective. Whether a mark signifies discipline, selflessness, leadership, spiritual growth, or resilience, it embodies a truth: These markings are not merely for the individual—they are for the group, the unity above all else.

0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
0.-worlds,-verses-&-settings/fera-world/.description:
The Parables of Eryndor were crafted with a singular purpose in mind: to cultivate virtues that would bind the Children of the Abandoned together in unity. Each parable carries a profound lesson, speaking directly to the heart of what it means to live not for oneself but for the collective. These are not mere stories—they are the very foundation of the Children’s philosophy, lessons to live by, to guide them in times of challenge, doubt, or uncertainty. Eryndor’s wisdom permeates these tales, beckoning each listener to hear the call to selflessness.


"It is the small, silent spokes that make the wheel turn."
In the earliest days of their wanderings, before the Children knew the meaning of true purpose, Eryndor gathered the group beside the warmth of the fire. The flames flickered against the deep chill of the night, casting shadows across their faces, where the light could only catch the edges of their forms. The time had come for a lesson.
They were in a strange land then, traversing through barren fields toward an unknown village. The Children had been pulling a wooden cart, one that Eryndor had built with his own hands. Though rough, it was sturdy, intended to carry them and their meager possessions on their travels.
One fateful evening, when the moon was clouded by shifting skies, Eryndor paused. The cart’s wheel had fractured—a great crack running through it. The weight of the journey had taken its toll, and now they would be forced to abandon the cart if they could not repair it.
Without hesitation, Eryndor addressed the Children. "This wheel is broken, just as we are in many ways. Alone, it is useless, just as a single soul may fall if it stands alone. But we shall not despair. Let us mend the wheel together."
A child named Coris stepped forward, asking, "But the wheel cannot turn with just one spoke, can it? We need every part of it to move forward."
Eryndor smiled and nodded. "True, but it is not the wheel that moves. It is the strength of the hands that carry it, and the unity of those hands that gives it its power. Each spoke—small, silent, humble—supports the wheel. We will all carry it as one. Each of you has something to give, even if you believe it is small. There is no work too insignificant, no hand too weak."
The Children gathered and, one by one, carefully and quietly began to mend the wheel, using wooden boards, nails, and whatever tools they had at their disposal. As the wheel was repaired, the group found that the cart, once broken, was stronger than before. The Children, bound by a simple, unspoken understanding, had proven that it was the unity of effort that brought them strength—not the prowess of a single individual.
From this moment on, it became etched into the very hearts of the Children that their purpose in this world was not to shine as individuals but to be a part of a whole. Without each one, no progress would be made. As Eryndor often said, “The strongest walls are those built by many hands.”


"There is no face behind the mask, for the face belongs only to the world."
Years after the Children began their sacred journey, Eryndor saw that the group had become strong, both in numbers and spirit. Yet, not all had embraced the principles of silence and unity that he had taught them. There were those who, in the secret corners of their hearts, still yearned for attention—who wished their individual merits to be recognized.
One day, as they traveled, a child named Elian approached him, bearing in his hands a polished mask—a mask so intricately carved that it gleamed even in the dimmest light. “Master Eryndor,” Elian said, his voice faltering slightly, “this is my face. I offer it to the world. With this mask, I will bring honor to our fellowship. I will do what others cannot.”
Eryndor took the mask carefully in his hands. The surface was decorated with the faces of people—some familiar, others unknown, their expressions captured in eternal permanence. It was a mask of grandeur, meant to showcase strength and pride, to tell the world of Elian’s accomplishments.
“No, Elian,” Eryndor said solemnly, “this mask is not yours to offer. It was given to you by the world, and it is a symbol of all you should leave behind.”
“But what harm does it cause to be known for my strength, to show the world what I can do?” Elian argued.
“Listen to me carefully, child,” Eryndor replied. “There is no face behind the mask, for the world will always seek to label you by what it sees. The mask hides your true self, turning you into something you were never meant to be: an object to be praised or scorned. If you seek the admiration of the world, you will find that it will consume you, just as fire consumes wood. But here, beneath the helmet, your worth is not for the world to judge—it belongs only to the collective. And in this unity, there is a far greater power than any praise can offer.”
Eryndor removed his own helmet and placed it into Elian’s hands. "This is your true face, and with it, you are one with the rest of us. In silence, we find our voice. Let your deeds speak, not your appearance. The world need never know your name. What matters is the strength you give to others, and in giving that strength, you shall find true purpose."
From that moment, Elian understood that the path of unity was not one of shining out but of standing firm within. To seek attention or glory was a temptation that must be cast aside if he was ever to truly find peace with his own heart. The Children of the Abandoned would never reveal their faces to the world, for their identities were forged in the bond between them, not in individual recognition.


"If we stand together, we are unbreakable."
Long before the Children settled in their first true home, there was a time when they wandered. The night was cold, the moon hidden behind dark clouds, and the path was uncertain. Their strength had already been tested time and again, but this night’s test would be different. The storm was fierce, a tempest of icy winds and roaring thunder. As they struggled forward, it became apparent that they could not continue at the same pace—they needed to find shelter quickly.
Eryndor paused the group and directed their gaze to the mountainside ahead of them. Among the trees, he pointed to a large stone resting at the edge of a precipice. The stone teetered on the edge, as if waiting to tumble into the chasm below.
"This stone is like us," Eryndor said. "Alone, it will fall. But together, we will move it. And together, we shall endure this storm."
The Children, though weary and cold, moved toward the stone, positioning themselves at its sides, each child grasping hold of the rock’s jagged surface. Slowly, patiently, they began to push, their hands working in unison. At first, there was no movement—no shift. But gradually, inch by inch, the stone shifted, as if acknowledging their combined will. When the stone finally lay in a safe place, secure and anchored in the earth, the Children turned toward Eryndor.
"Here is our lesson," he said, his voice firm, but soft against the winds. "This stone, alone, would have fallen and been lost to the world. But when we stand together, we are like the rock: unbreakable, unshakable. It is not our strength, individually, that keeps us whole, but our willingness to stand beside each other, to share the burden, no matter the weight. Together, we find the strength to face all storms."
In the days that followed, the storm passed, but the lesson stayed etched in their hearts: When we are united, no force can topple us. No storm, no hardship, no darkness is too great. In unity, we become unshakable.
